sections.title: Domain 4: Operational Efficiency and Optimization for GenAI Applications

keyTerms.definition: Pay-per-token Bedrock pricing with no commitment, where idle hours cost nothing.
Using the fewest tokens that still complete the job, the first free cost control.
Reserved Bedrock capacity bought per model unit per hour for one to six months.

recall.question: What trade-off does every Domain 4 scenario require?
recall.answer: Choosing between cost, latency, and quality, then picking the correct control for the scenario's limit.

recall.question: What is the volume's one-sentence summary of the levers?
recall.answer: On-demand charges per token for spiky traffic, token efficiency is the first free control, then retrieval tuning, prompt caching, semantic caching, batch, provisioned throughput, smaller models with routing, and fine-tuning last.

keyTerms.definition: The table that maps each scenario limit to one lever, worth memorizing before the rest of the domain.
A Bedrock feature that bills repeated static prompt prefixes at a discounted input rate.
An architecture that returns stored answers for repeated meanings without calling the model.
Reserved model capacity bought hourly for a one to six month term.

recall.question: What should you memorize before reading the rest of the domain?
recall.answer: The decision map, which answers half of the domain by mapping each scenario limit to one lever.

recall.question: What are the pricing controls in order?
recall.answer: Token efficiency, retrieval tuning, prompt caching, semantic caching, batch, provisioned throughput, smaller models and routers, then fine-tuning.

sections.title: 01. On-demand inference pricing and token economics

keyTerms.definition: Bedrock's pay-as-you-go pricing where you pay per token with zero cost when idle.
All data sent to the model, including the system prompt, history, tools, and user message.
All data the model generates, billed at a higher rate than input tokens.
Cost per call equals input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price.

recall.question: Why does the bill grow when nobody changes the model?
recall.answer: The whole conversation history is re-billed as input tokens on every turn, a silent multiplier.

recall.question: When is on-demand the cheapest choice?
recall.answer: When traffic is spiky, unpredictable, or low, because idle hours cost nothing while provisioned throughput charges for idle capacity.

keyTerms.definition: Using the fewest tokens that still complete the job, the free lever pulled first.
Removing irrelevant conversation history or document parts instead of resending them every call.
Rewriting long instructions as short ones without changing the meaning.
The inference setting that caps output length and limits output token spend.

recall.question: Why is token efficiency the first lever to use?
recall.answer: It costs nothing to use and it makes every other pricing lever work better.

recall.question: Why is prompt compression a process rather than a one-time change?
recall.answer: You must re-evaluate after each step, since removing too much history trades cost for wrong answers.

keyTerms.definition: A Bedrock pricing feature that discounts repeated static input tokens via a marked cache point.
The marker in the request before which Bedrock stores computed state for reuse.
Time to live, about five minutes by default, after which the cached prefix must be recomputed.
A small extra charge on the first call that writes the cached prefix state.

recall.question: What two things break prompt caching?
recall.answer: Any change to the prefix content before the cache point, and the TTL expiring between calls.

recall.question: Why is prompt caching the wrong fix for throttling?
recall.answer: It is a cost control that discounts repeated input tokens, not a capacity control, so peak throttling needs provisioned throughput or rate-limit handling.

keyTerms.definition: Storing model responses and reusing them for new questions that mean the same thing.
A numeric vector representing the meaning of a question for similarity comparison.
The similarity measure comparing a new question's embedding to cached embeddings.
The minimum similarity, for example 0.95, that counts a cached question as a hit.
The share of questions answered from cache, measured on real traffic before adopting the architecture.

recall.question: When does semantic caching fail?
recall.answer: When queries are highly personalized and unique, the hit rate collapses and the cache adds complexity for no savings.

recall.question: What is the key difference between semantic caching and prompt caching?
recall.answer: Semantic caching removes the call completely for repeated meanings, while prompt caching discounts input tokens on calls you still make.

keyTerms.definition: Using the fewest context tokens that still contain the answer, starting with the cheapest change.
The number of chunks the retriever returns per query, cut when the answer sits in the top few.
A small model that scores candidate chunks for relevance so only the best few reach the prompt.
Shrinking the candidate set by document metadata before vector search, needing a smaller top-k.

recall.question: What is the cheapest retrieval-tuning lever?
recall.answer: Lowering top-k, for example from 10 to 3 when the answer is always in the top three, cutting retrieval token cost by 70 percent.

recall.question: Why should you not add more chunks to fix wrong answers?
recall.answer: More chunks raise cost and often lower quality through noise, so fix retrieval with a lower top-k, reranking, or denser chunking.

sections.title: 06. Right-sizing models and cascading with routers

keyTerms.definition: Matching the model to the task's difficulty instead of using the flagship for everything.
Routing simple requests to a cheap model and escalating only complex ones to the flagship.
Bedrock's managed router that sends each prompt to the cheapest model that can handle it.
The low-confidence path that moves a request from the small model up to the flagship.

recall.question: What makes cascading cut the bill by about 70 percent?
recall.answer: A router sends 80 percent of traffic to a model 10 times cheaper with no measurable quality drop, but the router itself must be almost free.

recall.question: What is the real risk of a cascade?
recall.answer: Router misclassification sending hard questions to the small model, controlled by per-route quality monitoring and low-confidence escalation.

sections.title: 07. Fine-tuning a small model for your workload

keyTerms.definition: Training a model on labeled examples so a behavior becomes part of the weights, not the prompt.
Training a small cheap student model to imitate a large teacher model on one narrow task.
Reserved capacity, usually required before a fine-tuned custom model can be invoked at all.
Better training examples beat more examples, since the model learns your habits at scale.

recall.question: When does fine-tuning pay off?
recall.answer: Only for a narrow, repeated behavior with stable rules at huge volume, where one-time training plus the hourly serving commitment is smaller than the flagship tokens saved.

recall.question: Why is fine-tuning on changing documents wrong?
recall.answer: Documents that update monthly go stale in the weights and cannot cite sources, so that is RAG's job.

sections.title: 08. Latency vs throughput: streaming and perceived speed

keyTerms.definition: What users feel, driven by time to first token rather than total generation time.
Time to first token, the delay before the first token appears including prompt processing.
Sending tokens as the model generates them, so users see words in about a second.
The delay until the last token, which streaming does not change.
The randomness control, where 0 is the most deterministic setting, not a cost control.

recall.question: What is the difference between perceived latency and total latency?
recall.answer: Perceived latency is time to first token and total latency is time to the last token, so streaming improves perception without changing total generation time.

recall.question: Why is streaming alone wrong for a hard sub-3-second SLA?
recall.answer: Streaming changes when the user sees output, not total time, so the guarantee needs a smaller model plus provisioned throughput plus streaming.

keyTerms.definition: Bedrock's asynchronous discounted inference mode, about half price with hours of latency.
The file format for batch input, with one complete model invocation per line.
The API that starts a batch job with an input S3 URI and an output S3 URI.
The idle capacity windows AWS schedules batch work into, which is why batch costs less.

recall.question: What is the batch inference price and latency trade?
recall.answer: About 50 percent lower than on-demand for the same model, but results arrive hours later with no latency SLA.

recall.question: What is the main batch trap on the exam?
recall.answer: Using batch for an interactive workload to save money, since hours-scale latency breaks the product even though the discount is real.

keyTerms.definition: Reserved inference capacity on Bedrock bought per model unit per hour for one to six months.
The purchase unit of provisioned capacity, each with fixed processing capacity for one model.
The identifier your code must invoke to use reserved capacity, not the base model ID.
Policies that add or remove model units as utilization crosses thresholds, within set limits.
Provisioned Throughput for the predictable baseline plus on-demand overflow for spikes.

recall.question: What is the exam's most correct production pattern for steady traffic with spikes?
recall.answer: Provisioned Throughput for the predictable baseline plus on-demand overflow for spikes, provisioning for the floor and never the peak.

recall.question: Why does throttling continue after buying provisioned throughput?
recall.answer: The code still calls the base model ID instead of the provisioned model ARN, so traffic stays on the on-demand pool.

keyTerms.definition: A Bedrock routing identifier that sends a request to a model in one of several regions.
The us., eu., apac., and global. profile prefixes that route within data-residency boundaries.
A self-created profile wrapping one region or system profile that adds tags and metrics.
The scope decision keeping data inside required regions, such as EU data in EU regions.

recall.question: How do inference profiles improve resilience?
recall.answer: They pool capacity across regions with automatic failover, so a throttled region retries in another profile region transparently.

recall.question: How do you distinguish the three routing concepts?
recall.answer: Inference profiles route across regions for availability, prompt routers route by complexity for cost, and provisioned throughput reserves capacity.

sections.title: 12. Rate limits, quotas, and throttling with retries

keyTerms.definition: AWS rejecting requests above the quota, a signal to slow down rather than a bug.
The error Bedrock returns when a client exceeds its request quota.
Waiting longer before each retry, about 1 second, then 2, then 4, until attempts run out.
A small random offset added to each wait so many clients do not retry at once.
API Gateway rate limits and API keys that protect the backend from client bursts.

recall.question: How should a client handle ThrottlingException?
recall.answer: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, waiting about 1 second, then 2, then 4, with a random offset so clients do not retry together.

recall.question: When is a quota increase the wrong answer?
recall.answer: During brief sub-minute spikes, which retries absorb, since quota increases are for sustained legitimate growth.

keyTerms.definition: The CloudWatch metric for the number of model calls, your volume baseline.
The CloudWatch metric for input tokens, your cost baseline with OutputTokenCount.
The CloudWatch metric for output tokens, where a 3x jump with flat invocations means longer responses.
The CloudWatch metric counting throttled requests, signaling quota limits.
CloudWatch machine-learning baselines that flag unusual spikes without manual thresholds.

recall.question: What does an OutputTokenCount spike with flat invocations mean?
recall.answer: Responses became longer, a prompt or maxTokens regression, not a traffic or capacity problem.

recall.question: Which tools are wrong for token-spend and quality monitoring?
recall.answer: CloudTrail, the audit plane without token counts, and SageMaker Model Monitor, which is for tabular ML and not GenAI text.

sections.title: 14. Model invocation logging and X-Ray tracing

keyTerms.definition: Recording full Bedrock request and response bodies to S3 or CloudWatch Logs for forensics.
Distributed tracing that follows one request across services and records each step's timing.
The identifier given to each request so every service call becomes a timed segment.
The encryption expected on invocation log destinations for healthcare and finance workloads.
The query tool for searching invocation logs to find expensive or long responses.

recall.question: What question does each observability plane answer?
recall.answer: Metrics show what moved, invocation logs show what was said, and traces show where the time went.

recall.question: What must a healthcare team do about invocation logs?
recall.answer: Encrypt the destination with KMS or disable logging, since raw prompts and responses can contain PII.

keyTerms.definition: The ordered list of optimization levers from the cheapest free actions to the most expensive commitments.
The exam's most correct pattern, matching each traffic shape to its own pricing lever.
The ladder's first step, using CloudWatch metrics and anomaly detection before optimizing.
The latency lever that shows tokens as they arrive, improving perceived speed.

recall.question: What is the ladder rule for exam answers?
recall.answer: The correct answer is the cheapest action that fits the scenario's limits, so go down the ladder and never up.

recall.question: What comes after fine-tuning on the cost ladder?
recall.answer: Defer with batch inference, guarantee with provisioned throughput, route with inference profiles, then stream, retry, and govern spend.

sections.title: Questions: Topic 01, On-demand pricing and token economics

keyTerms.definition: Pay-per-token pricing with no commitment, cheapest for spiky or experimental traffic.
Reserved capacity with an hourly fee for the full term, paid whether used or not.
Async S3-based inference at about half price, unsuitable for interactive chat.
The CloudWatch metric for input tokens, analyzed per tenant for chargeback.

recall.question: A startup prototypes a chat feature with unpredictable usage. Which pricing model is correct?
recall.answer: On-demand inference, because it charges only for tokens used and idle hours cost nothing, while provisioned throughput would charge hourly for quiet days.

recall.question: What is the approximate monthly saving of cascading 3M calls with 85 percent on a lightweight model?
recall.answer: About $21,000, from $27,000 all-flagship down to about $5,962.50 cascaded.

keyTerms.definition: Removing input tokens from every call, for example keeping only recent turns.
An optimization loop of shrinking the prompt, evaluating, and stopping when quality changes.
The setting that limits output tokens per call, paired with concise-answer instructions.
A sampling control that changes diversity, not token counts or cost.

recall.question: A chatbot sends 3,000 tokens of history every call. What is the simplest cost cut?
recall.answer: Use the last 6 turns or summarize older turns, since context pruning removes input tokens from every call at no cost.

recall.question: Which two changes improve RAG token use without hurting quality?
recall.answer: Get fewer, better-ranked chunks with hybrid search and reranking, and shorten the instruction text around the chunks.

keyTerms.definition: The Bedrock feature discounting repeated input tokens before a cache point.
The Converse marker that makes the prefix the cached portion.
The cache lifetime, about five minutes by default, expiring between infrequent calls.
Reuses of the cached prefix, lost when anything before the cache point changes.

recall.question: An agent resends a 10,000-token tool spec every turn. What cuts the input-token cost?
recall.answer: Prompt caching with a cache point before the tool specification, since the same static text repeats many times.

recall.question: Why did prompt caching produce almost no cache hits when the timestamp sits at the start?
recall.answer: Any change before the cache point invalidates the cache, so move the dynamic fields after the cache point to keep the prefix identical.

keyTerms.definition: A layer before the model that matches questions by meaning and skips the call.
The matching line, raised when users get answers to similar but different questions.
The share of repeated questions served from cache, collapsing when queries are unique.
The store giving sub-millisecond lookups for the hot cache path.

recall.question: A FAQ bot gets millions of repeated questions in different words. What reduces cost and latency?
recall.answer: A semantic cache with similarity matching in front of the model, since hits skip the model call completely.

recall.question: Why will semantic caching fail for a personalized recommendation engine?
recall.answer: Each query is unique to a user, so the hit rate collapses and the cache adds complexity with no savings.

keyTerms.definition: The chunk count per query, lowered when the answer sits in the top few chunks.
Scoring candidates by relevance and keeping only the top few for the prompt.
The re-check after tuning that guards answer quality on a golden test set.
Shrinking candidates by document date before vector search.

recall.question: A RAG app sends 10 chunks of 500 tokens but the answer is usually in the top 3. What is the cheapest first step?
recall.answer: Make top-k 3 from 10 and re-evaluate, removing 70 percent of retrieval tokens for no cost.

recall.question: What is the correct fix when cutting top-k from 10 to 3 drops accuracy from 92 to 81 percent?
recall.answer: Retrieve broadly, rerank with precision, and truncate, since recall is good at top 10 but precision at top 3 lost the answer chunk.

keyTerms.definition: Routing simple queries to a cheap model and complex ones to the flagship.
The classifier whose cost must be almost free compared to the calls it routes.
The low-confidence path moving requests up to the flagship model.
The router sending complex questions to the small model, fixed by better criteria.

recall.question: 80 percent of requests are simple FAQ lookups on an expensive flagship. What is the most cost-effective change?
recall.answer: Route simple queries to the lightweight model and keep complex ones on the flagship, saving about 10x per-token cost on most traffic.

recall.question: What is wrong when the router model costs as much as the flagship?
recall.answer: The router cost can erase the savings, so the router must be almost free, such as rules, a small model, or the managed prompt router.

keyTerms.definition: The last lever, for stable narrow repetition at very high volume.
Copying a teacher's behavior into a small student model for a narrow task.
The hourly serving commitment usually needed to invoke a custom model.
The one-time cost paid back only when monthly volume is large enough.

recall.question: A company sends 50M responses a month with a large stable brand-voice prompt. What is most correct?
recall.answer: Fine-tune a small model on brand-voice examples so the style lives in the weights and the prompt shrinks.

recall.question: Why is distilling the 800k per month classifier wrong at $0.006 per flagship call?
recall.answer: The distilled serving cost is $400 plus $14,400 per month for provisioned throughput, totaling $14,800, more than the current $4,800.

keyTerms.definition: Tokens shown one by one, the fix for a chatbot that feels slow.
Time to first token, lowered by a smaller model or prompt caching.
Guaranteed capacity for a hard sub-3-second SLA, not perception.
What streaming improves, without changing total generation time.

recall.question: Users say a chatbot feels slow with correct answers taking 10 seconds. What is the first change?
recall.answer: Turn on streaming with ConverseStream so tokens show one by one, since it is a perceived-latency problem.

recall.question: Which two actions lower time to first token for a voice assistant?
recall.answer: Use a smaller model for faster tokens and prompt caching to skip prefix recomputation.

keyTerms.definition: S3 input and output at about 50 percent off for offline work.
The line-per-request file format, where a small error fraction means malformed lines.
The role giving Bedrock read access to input and write access to output S3 locations.
The storage for batch input files and output results as JSONL.

recall.question: A media company must classify 500,000 tickets in 24 hours. What is the most cost-effective method?
recall.answer: Batch inference with S3 input and output, about 50 percent less than on-demand.

recall.question: A batch job finishes with 2 percent line errors on a 100,000-line JSONL. What is the fix?
recall.answer: Individual lines were malformed, so fix those lines and resubmit only those lines.

keyTerms.definition: Reserved hourly capacity, sized for the baseline with on-demand overflow for peaks.
The capacity purchase unit, added by autoscaling when utilization crosses a threshold.
The identifier calls must use, or traffic stays on the throttled on-demand pool.
Adding or removing units within minimum and maximum bounds as the API grows.

recall.question: A team bought provisioned throughput but throttles continue on the base model ID. What is wrong?
recall.answer: The application still uses the base model ID instead of the provisioned model ARN, so buying capacity does not help until routing changes.

recall.question: Why is sizing provisioned throughput for the 2,000 RPM Friday spike wrong?
recall.answer: PT bills 24/7, so reserving peak capacity for a 4-hour weekly spike pays peak prices for about 164 idle hours, and the correct design provisions the 300 RPM floor.

sections.title: Questions: Topic 11, Inference profiles and routing

keyTerms.definition: Cross-region routing with automatic failover, called by profile ID.
Complexity-based routing for cost and quality, distinct from profiles.
The compliance decision, for example the eu. prefix keeping EU data in EU regions.
Raising the ceiling for sustained growth, one way to add capacity without rewriting code.

recall.question: A model is in only two regions and the app needs failover with minimal code changes. What must it call?
recall.answer: The inference profile ID, for example with a us. prefix, which routes across regions and fails over automatically.

recall.question: A healthcare app must keep inference data inside the EU. Which prefix is correct?
recall.answer: The eu. prefix, which limits routing to EU regions, since global. could route anywhere.

sections.title: Questions: Topic 12, Rate limits, quotas, retries

keyTerms.definition: The error during short spikes, fixed with SDK retries rather than provisioned throughput.
Waiting 1 second, then 2, then 4, spreading retries over time.
The random offset stopping synchronized retry waves across thousands of clients.
Per-method rate limits and usage plans protecting the backend at the edge.

recall.question: An app gets ThrottlingException during spikes under one minute. What is the smallest correct fix?
recall.answer: SDK retries with exponential backoff and jitter, the default SDK behavior for temporary spikes.

recall.question: Which two structural actions fix a hard, hours-long overload?
recall.answer: Set provisioned throughput for the long baseline or ask AWS Support for a quota increase, since retries cannot fix sustained overload.

keyTerms.definition: The managed near-real-time view of token spend and throttling with minimal work.
Learning normal patterns and flagging deviations without manual thresholds.
The token metric showing spend, missed by static alarms on invocations alone.
The audit plane, wrong for performance or cost monitoring.

recall.question: OutputTokenCount tripled while invocations and throttles are flat. What is the most probable cause?
recall.answer: Responses became longer, since a prompt change removed length limits or raised maxTokens, not a capacity shortage.

recall.question: Which two mistakes does the exam test in monitoring?
recall.answer: Using CloudTrail for token-spend monitoring and SageMaker Model Monitor for GenAI text quality drift, instead of CloudWatch and Bedrock evaluations.

sections.title: Questions: Topic 14, Invocation logging and tracing

keyTerms.definition: Bedrock model invocation logging records request and response bodies for forensics.
Distributed tracing showing timing for each step of a multi-step agent.
The expected protection for invocation logs containing PII in regulated workloads.
Records who called which API, but never prompt or response bodies.

recall.question: A team must audit the exact prompts and responses for a cost spike. What must they enable?
recall.answer: Bedrock model invocation logging to S3 or CloudWatch Logs, the prompt forensics plane.

recall.question: Which two steps find the problem when an agent gives wrong answers sometimes?
recall.answer: Turn on agent tracing with enableTrace to see reasoning steps and tool calls, and query invocation logs in CloudWatch Logs Insights for the failing prompts and responses.

keyTerms.definition: Each workload gets its matching lever, the exam's most correct multi-constraint answer.
Set to 0 for consistency, since capacity tools do not control randomness.
The ordered levers, cheapest free actions first, committed capacity last.
The interactive lever for the chatbot, never for batch work.

recall.question: What portfolio serves a chatbot, a nightly job, and a steady API with an SLA?
recall.answer: Streaming plus right-sized models for the chatbot, batch inference for the nightly job, and provisioned throughput for the steady API.

recall.question: Which two orderings follow the optimization ladder correctly?
recall.answer: Measure, prune the prompt, then consider caching, cascading, batch, and provisioned throughput, and skip calls with semantic cache before discounting tokens with prompt caching.
